c.tagline: Mindanao's orderly gateway city — durian, Philippine eagles, Samal Island and towering Mount Apo.

taxi.fareNote: Davao strictly enforces taxi meters and its drivers are widely known for honesty and for returning lost belongings; Grab and the local Micab app are also widely available.

emergency.note: 911 is the nationwide emergency number; Davao also runs its own Central 911 command center, one of the first in the country, with generally good English response.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

solo.f: Women's-safety index (WPS) is the main factor (61/100)

avoid.reason: Well-policed city, but wider Mindanao has security risks — check advisories

hood_desc: The historic downtown core around San Pedro Cathedral, People's Park, the City Hall and the old public markets; the central, walkable base for first-timers who want the city's landmarks, government offices and cheapest eats close at hand.

The business and shopping spine along J.P. Laurel Avenue north of downtown, anchored by the Abreeza Ayala mall and lined with hotels, offices and restaurants; a convenient, upscale-leaning base within easy reach of the center.

The upmarket coastal district northeast toward the airport, home to SM Lanang Premier, beachfront hotels and the Insular waterfront; a quieter, resort-and-mall area popular with business and leisure visitors.

A busy residential and dining district south of downtown, centred on Matina Town Square off McArthur Highway - a walled compound of live-music bars, grills and casual restaurants that fills up in the evening; a lively, local place to eat and go out.

The compact old Chinatown around Uyanguren (Ramon Magsaysay Avenue), packed with Chinese-Filipino eateries, durian stalls, temples and bustling street commerce; a flavorful, walkable pocket for food and shopping.

water.note: Davao's tap water is rated among the Philippines' best and is generally safe, though sensitive stomachs may prefer bottled.

transit.hours: Jeepneys and the new city buses run roughly 5:00 AM to around 10:00 PM; late at night, taxis, Grab and Micab are the reliable options.
transit.note: Davao has no rail or metro; public transport is built on jeepneys and, increasingly, the modern High Priority Bus System (HPBS) that is replacing many old routes, supplemented by metered taxis and Grab.
transit.pay: Jeepney and bus fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor (fares start around 13-15 pesos); there is no city-wide smartcard yet, while Grab and Micab are paid in-app or in cash.

tip.r: Tipping is appreciated but modest; leaving around 10% at restaurants without a service charge, and small change for guides, drivers and hotel staff, is customary.

food.name: Grilled Tuna Panga
food.desc: The prized jaw of yellowfin tuna, marinated and charcoal-grilled until the skin blisters, served with soy-calamansi and chili dip.

places.name: Luz Kinilaw Place
places.note: Nearly 50-year-old grill house; panga cooked over coals in front of you, eaten with your hands.

places.name: Marina Tuna Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Serves tuna a dozen ways; the panga and belly are the reason locals bring visitors here.

places.name: Yellow Fin Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Bright, family-friendly seafood hall known for consistently fresh grilled tuna belly and panga.

food.name: Kinilaw na Tuna
food.desc: Davao's answer to ceviche: raw tuna cured in coconut vinegar and calamansi with ginger, onion, chili and sometimes coconut milk.

places.name: Luz Kinilaw Place
places.note: The city's benchmark kinilaw, cut thick and sharply sour; the dish the place is named for.

places.name: Marina Tuna Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Classic vinegar-and-ginger version made from the same tuna they grill and serve as sashimi.

places.name: Ahfat Seafood Plaza
places.note: Long-running Chinese-Filipino seafood institution; kinilaw ordered alongside big shared platters.

food.name: Sinuglaw
food.desc: A Mindanao mash-up of sinugba (grilled pork belly) and kinilaw, smoky and rich against sour cured fish in one bowl.

places.name: Luz Kinilaw Place
places.note: Grill and kinilaw under one roof, so the pork arrives hot and the fish stays cold and tart.

places.name: Yellow Fin Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Generous sinuglaw platter that works well as a shared starter before the grilled seafood.

places.name: Roxas Night Market
places.note: Street stalls plate cheap sinuglaw beside charcoal grills; go early evening for the freshest batch.

food.name: Sinigang na Tuna Belly
food.desc: Fatty tuna belly simmered in a tamarind-soured broth with kangkong, radish and tomato; the everyday comfort dish of Davao households.

places.name: Marina Tuna Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Signature sour broth with thick belly cuts; among the most ordered dishes on the menu.

places.name: Ahfat Seafood Plaza
places.note: Big-format sinigang built for groups, a Davao family-celebration standard for decades.

places.name: Yellow Fin Seafood Restaurant
places.note: Clean, tamarind-forward version that pairs well with their buttered shrimp and rice.

food.name: Durian
food.desc: Davao is the durian capital of the Philippines; eat it fresh by the kilo or tamed into ice cream, candy, tarts and cheesecake.

places.name: Magsaysay Park fruit stands
places.note: Rows of vendors selling Puyat and Arancillo durian; they open and let you taste before buying.

places.name: Bankerohan Public Market
places.note: The city's main produce market; cheapest fresh durian in season plus candies and jams.

places.name: Lachi's Sans Rival Atbp
places.note: Local bakeshop famous for durian cheesecake and tarts if the fresh fruit is too much.

food.name: Pomelo and Davao fruit plate
food.desc: Sweet-tart Davao pomelo alongside mangosteen, marang, lanzones and Cavendish banana, the region's other agricultural claim to fame.

places.name: Bankerohan Public Market
places.note: Best prices and widest selection; ask vendors to segment the pomelo for you.

places.name: Magsaysay Park fruit stands
places.note: Convenient central row of stalls with mangosteen and marang alongside the durian.

places.name: Roxas Night Market
places.note: Fruit vendors work the market edges after dark, handy for a light dessert after grilled food.

food.name: Durian shake
food.desc: Blended fresh durian with milk and ice, thick as a milkshake; the gentlest way into the fruit for first-timers.

places.name: Magsaysay Park fruit stands
places.note: Stalls blend shakes to order from the same fruit they are selling whole.

places.name: Roxas Night Market
places.note: Cheap shakes served in cups at the night market, a Davao evening ritual.

places.name: Lachi's Sans Rival Atbp
places.note: Air-conditioned option for a durian shake plus durian pastries in one sitting.

food.name: Sikwate (tablea hot chocolate)
food.desc: Thick, barely sweet hot chocolate whisked from local cacao tablea; Davao grows some of Asia's most awarded cacao.

places.name: Malagos Chocolate Cafe
places.note: Cafe of the award-winning Davao estate; single-origin drinking chocolate and bars.

places.name: Malagos Garden Resort
places.note: The farm itself, with a chocolate museum and tastings straight from the source.

places.name: Bankerohan Public Market
places.note: Buy raw tablea discs by the bag from market stalls at a fraction of cafe prices.

landmarks: San Pedro Cathedral
Davao's oldest church, founded in 1847 and rebuilt with a striking wave-shaped modernist facade, anchors the historic heart beside city hall.
People's Park
A downtown showcase of indigenous-themed sculptures by Kublai Millan, dancing fountains and gardens celebrating Mindanao's Lumad and Moro cultures.
Jack's Ridge
A hillside dining-and-viewpoint complex on a former Japanese wartime stronghold, famous for sparkling night panoramas over the city and gulf.
Roxas Night Market
Every evening Roxas Avenue erupts with sizzling barbecue, durian stalls and bargain massages, the tastiest crash course in Davao street life.
Davao Crocodile Park
Home to the giant saltwater crocs and Mindanaoan wildlife, with feeding shows and an adjacent cultural village and butterfly house.
D' Bone Collector Museum
An eccentric downtown museum displaying thousands of skeletons, from sperm whales to snakes, assembled into a quirky lesson on biodiversity.
Magsaysay Park
A waterfront park on Davao Gulf centered on a tri-pillar obelisk honoring President Ramon Magsaysay, a favorite spot for riverside strolls, exercise classes and sunset views.
Bankerohan Public Market
Davao's biggest and oldest public market, a maze of stalls piled with durian, mangosteen and other tropical produce alongside everyday household goods.
Shrine of the Holy Infant Jesus of Prague (Shrine Hills)
A hilltop pilgrimage church in Matina housing a replica of Prague's revered Holy Infant statue, with a lookout offering sweeping views over Davao Gulf.
Davao Chinatown (Uyanguren)
The bustling Chinese-Filipino quarter along Ramon Magsaysay Avenue, marked by ornamental archways and packed with wholesale shops, street food and Lunar New Year festivities.

train.note: Mindanao has no operating railway of any kind, so there are no trains to or from Davao. Philippine National Railways (https://pnr.gov.ph/) runs only in Luzon - the Metro North Commuter around Manila and the reopened Naga-Legazpi section of the Bicol line. The long-promised Mindanao Railway Project, whose first phase would link Tagum, Davao and Digos, has been repeatedly redesigned and refinanced and no track is in service. Until it is built, buses along the Pan-Philippine Highway and domestic flights are the only options.

bus.note: Long-distance buses leave the Davao Overland Transport Terminal and Ecoland Terminal for cities across Mindanao — Cagayan de Oro, General Santos, Butuan, Surigao and Cotabato among them. There are no international bus services.

ferry.note: Frequent barges and small boats cross to Samal Island (the Island Garden City of Samal) from the Sasa and Sta. Ana wharves in just 10-15 minutes, and passenger ferries and larger 2GO ships link Davao's Sasa port with Manila and other domestic ports across the Davao Gulf. There are no international ferry routes.

half.name: Samal Island (IGaCoS)
half.blurb: A resort island of white-sand beaches, the Monfort bat cave and snorkeling, just a short barge ride across the gulf (~15 min by boat).

full.name: Mount Apo
full.blurb: The Philippines' highest peak, a multi-day trek through mossy forest, boulder fields and a summit crater (trailheads ~1.5-2 hr).

full.name: Kapatagan / Mount Apo foothills
full.blurb: Highland farms, waterfalls and cool viewpoints on the Davao del Sur side of Apo, an easier taste of the mountain (~2 hr).
